channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Attackers crossed from a wind farm into an unrelated Polish CHP plant over a private cellular APN — and stopped its steam turbine
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed on 8 August that a December 2025 intrusion at a small Polish combined heat and power plant, which supplies heat to roughly 50,000 residents, was reached through a private cellular APN. It is the first observed case of that path into an OT network. Because the distribution operator’s private APN allowed arbitrary devices on it to talk to one another, the attacker pivoted from a compromised wind-farm network to a controller at an unrelated CHP site and shut down the steam turbine and the water treatment system. Staff did not recognise it as an attack for months, assuming contractor error during concurrent maintenance. For utilities the lesson is uncomfortable: private APNs, widely recommended as a safer alternative to internet exposure, isolate a site only as well as their peer-to-peer rules do. - CERT Polska (NASK) follow-up report — corroborated by BleepingComputer and Help Net Security - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska report published 8 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] The second Polish plant went unrecognised for months — on the same day 30-plus renewable sites were hit
item.description: The CHP plant disclosed this month was not the only Polish energy target on 29 December 2025. Polish authorities said the same day saw coordinated activity against more than 30 renewable energy installations and a larger heat plant, which were disclosed in January. The smaller CHP plant reported its disruption “for informational purposes only” because maintenance was under way and staff assumed a contractor error; it took a CERT Polska investigation of more than three months to establish it was an intrusion. For power operators the detection failure is the transferable finding: a turbine trip during a maintenance window is exactly the condition under which a cyber cause is least likely to be considered. - The Record, citing CERT Polska - Reported 11 Aug 2026 (incident 29 Dec 2025)

item.title: [High] The Iranian-affiliated PLC campaign is not water-only — energy and municipal gas systems are named in scope
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-097A, issued in April by the FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA, DOE, Cyber National Mission Force and Treasury and updated on 22 July, describes Iranian-affiliated actors reaching internet-exposed PLCs across multiple US critical infrastructure sectors — water and wastewater, energy and government or municipal environments. The activity continues: utilities in at least 12 states have reported incidents since late July, and in Childersburg, Alabama the targeted operator runs water, sewer and gas together. Combined municipal utilities are the exposure most power-sector readers should check first, because a single small operations team often shares remote access, credentials and cellular routers across all three services. The July update also expanded observed vendor scope beyond Rockwell to Schneider Electric and Siemens PLCs. - CISA/FBI joint advisory AA26-097A — corroborated by SecurityWeek - Advisory 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; campaign incidents through 14 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 — and no operator touched a control system
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent from 1,020 in Q1, with North America accounting for 514. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them; organisations that support ICS environments — integrators, engineering firms, service providers — took another 117. The finding that matters for generation and transmission is what did not happen: Dragos observed no ransomware operator directly manipulating an industrial control system during the quarter. Disruption came from encrypted enterprise IT and from precautionary shutdowns of virtualisation and shared infrastructure. Your outage risk from ransomware is therefore mostly a question of how cleanly you can run the plant with the business network dark, and how many OT dependencies quietly live on shared hypervisors. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Gunra ransomware is walking in through unpatched VPNs and firewalls, and utilities are named in scope
item.description: The FBI, CISA, DoD Cyber Crime Center, NSA, US Secret Service and the Republic of Korea’s National Police Agency issued #StopRansomware advisory AA26-222A on Gunra, a double-extortion operation derived from leaked Conti source that moved to a structured affiliate model in early 2026. Its victim base explicitly includes utilities, manufacturing and transport. The initial access is not novel: affiliates are exploiting known authentication-bypass flaws in Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy — CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 — along with exposed RDP and other edge infrastructure. For a utility, the practical read is that the box most likely to start your next incident is the remote-access appliance in front of the corporate network, not anything inside the electronic security perimeter. - CISA #StopRansomware advisory AA26-222A - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A suspected China-nexus actor is mass-exploiting a patched vCenter flaw — the layer many OT DMZs sit on
item.description: Researchers have tied exploitation of CVE-2026-59310, a directory-traversal flaw in Broadcom VMware vCenter rated CVSS 9.8 and patched on 29 July, to a suspected China-nexus actor. German incident-response firm QUIRSO tracked roughly 361 unique victim IP addresses across 47 countries, with 343 appearing within the first three days of August; it assesses with moderate confidence that the operator is Chinese-speaking. The attack chain establishes persistence through cron, systemd and the reverse_ssh tool, drops a backdoor, and in some cases deploys Babuk-derived ransomware. Utilities should care because historians, HMIs, jump hosts and OT DMZ services are routinely virtualised: root on vCenter is root on the hypervisor carrying those workloads, and that is precisely the precautionary-shutdown scenario Dragos described. - The Hacker News, reporting QUIRSO research - Reported 17 Aug 2026 (patch 29 Jul 2026)

item.title: [Critical] August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 leads ten Siemens advisories
item.description: Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact published their August ICS Patch Tuesday bundles. Siemens issued ten new advisories, the most serious a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges on the underlying server. IoT2050 gateways are common in generation and substation edge deployments as data-collection and protocol-translation nodes, which puts them squarely between the plant network and whatever cloud or enterprise service they feed. There is no reported exploitation yet, and this is normal patch-and-monitor work rather than an emergency — but an unauthenticated remote code execution path on an edge gateway is worth pulling forward in the maintenance queue. - SecurityWeek, summarising Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories - Published 11–12 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway carries an unauthenticated root command-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an OS command-injection vulnerability in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway rated CVSS 10.0. The Net Check feature reachable through the /setting endpoint fails to sanitise input passed to the cmdPing Socket.io event, so an attacker can execute arbitrary operating-system commands as root. CISA lists Energy, Critical Manufacturing and Water and Wastewater among the affected sectors. Haiwell has published fixed firmware. These low-cost HMI and cloud-gateway products turn up in small generation sites, balance-of-plant systems and contractor-installed remote monitoring far more often than asset registers suggest, and they are frequently the device someone put on a cellular router so it could be checked from a phone. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-02 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA published 15 ICS advisories in a single day, several of them squarely energy-sector
item.description: CISA released 15 industrial control system advisories on 13 August, following three on 11 August and two on 4 August. Several land directly on energy asset owners: Johnson Controls Airwall, the Hitachi Energy APM Edge product, and ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA are all listed under the Energy sector. Separately, Hitachi Energy has issued updated mitigations for flaws in the Relion 670/650 and SAM600-IO protection relay families involving web interfaces and authentication flows that could allow tampering with protection and automation settings. None of these carries reported exploitation, so this is scheduled maintenance work — but relay and asset-performance platforms are the systems where a configuration change does the most damage, so treat the protection-relay items as the priority. - CISA ICS advisories, 13 Aug 2026 batch - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and FTD join CISA’s KEV catalogue for an actively exploited flaw
item.description: CISA added three vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August, including CVE-2026-20349, a heap inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense. The other two were CVE-2026-68820 in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection flaw in Metabase. The ASA/FTD entry is the one that matters for utilities: these appliances commonly terminate the corporate VPN, sit at the IT/OT boundary, or front vendor remote access into substation and plant networks. KEV listing means exploitation is confirmed in the wild, which puts this in the same category as the Fortinet flaws in the Gunra advisory — edge devices, known bugs, no sophistication required. - CISA KEV catalogue update - Added 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] CIP-015-1 internal network security monitoring: the first compliance date is 1 October 2028
item.description: CIP-015-1, the NERC reliability standard requiring internal network security monitoring inside the electronic security perimeter, is in force with staged compliance dates. High- and medium-impact BES Cyber Systems with external routable connectivity must implement INSM by 1 October 2028; all other BES Cyber Systems with ERC have until 1 October 2030. The requirements cover collecting network data feeds, detecting anomalous activity, evaluating what is detected, protecting the monitoring data itself and retaining investigation records. FERC has also directed NERC to extend the standard’s scope to EACMS and PACS outside the ESP. The Polish CHP case is a fair argument for not waiting: the plant lacked the internal visibility to distinguish an intrusion from a maintenance error for three months. - Dragos guidance on CIP-015-1, citing FERC Order and NERC standard - Compliance dates: 1 Oct 2028 (high/medium with ERC), 1 Oct 2030 (other)

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations begin in September 2026 for product manufacturers
item.description: From September 2026, manufacturers covered by the EU Cyber Resilience Act must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and serious security incidents in their products. For European energy operators this is a supply-side change rather than a new obligation of their own, but it should improve the quality and timeliness of disclosure from equipment vendors. It stacks on top of NIS2, under which electricity generation, transmission and distribution, district heating, gas and hydrogen are essential entities, and on the sector-specific Network Code on Cybersecurity (EU 2024/1366), which adds critical-impact classification, recurring union-wide risk assessments and cross-border crisis-management duties. The NIS2 Cooperation Group adopted common incident-reporting templates on 26 May 2026. - Reed Smith EU cybersecurity regulatory update - CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026
